The researchers developed DeepCNF, a deep learning framework that combines hierarchical convolutional neural networks with conditional random fields to model both complex sequence-structure relationships and dependencies between adjacent labels. This method achieved a Q3 accuracy of ~84% and a Q8 accuracy of ~72% on CASP and CAMEO test proteins, significantly outperforming previous predictors.

title: SidechainNet: An All-Atom Protein Structure Dataset for Machine Learning
authors: Jonathan E. King, David Ryan Koes
reason: Provides a key all-atom dataset used for training models that predict both backbone and sidechain, supporting the structural prediction task.
summary: Current protein structure prediction models often overlook the simultaneous modeling of backbone and sidechain information. The researchers developed SidechainNet, a new dataset that extends ProteinNet by providing angle and atomic coordinate data for all heavy atoms in protein structures. This dataset, accompanied by a dedicated software package, enables machine learning models to more accurately represent and predict complete all-atom protein structures.

title:
FoldExplorer: Fast and Accurate Protein Structure Search with
  Sequence-Enhanced Graph Embedding
authors: Yuan Liu and Hong-Bin Shen
reason: Focuses on structural homology search/retrieval using embeddings, which is a downstream task of structure prediction, but not prediction/design itself.
summary: Traditional protein structure search methods are too slow to handle the massive influx of data from modern prediction tools. FoldExplorer addresses this by using graph attention neural networks and protein large language models to create sequence-enhanced structural embeddings for rapid comparison. The method improves performance over current state-of-the-art algorithms by 5% to 8% while maintaining high search speeds on large-scale datasets.

title:
Protein sequence-to-structure learning: Is this the end(-to-end
  revolution)?
authors: Elodie Laine, Stephan Eismann, Arne Elofsson, and Sergei Grudinin

summary: This paper reviews the recent evolution of deep learning in protein structure prediction, specifically focusing on the transition toward end-to-end differentiable architectures. The review concludes that these diverse approaches, which collectively drove the near-experimental accuracy seen in CASP14, represent a significant shift in how protein sequences are mapped to 3D structures.

title:
Protein Secondary Structure Prediction Using Cascaded Convolutional and
  Recurrent Neural Networks
authors: Zhen Li and Yizhou Yu

summary: Predicting protein secondary structure is challenging due to the need to capture both local patterns and long-range amino acid dependencies. The researchers developed an end-to-end deep network that combines multi-scale convolutional neural networks for local features with bidirectional gated recurrent units for global context, using multi-task learning to simultaneously predict solvent accessibility. The model achieved state-of-the-art results with Q8 accuracies of 69.7% on CB513, 76.9% on CASP10, and 73.1% on CASP11.

title: Adaptive Protein Design Protocols and Middleware
authors: Aymen Alsaadi, Jonathan Ash, Mikhail Titov, Matteo Turilli, Andre Merzky, Shantenu Jha, Sagar Khare
reason: Discusses recent advancements in AI-driven protein design protocols and the infrastructure needed to scale them, representing the current edge.
summary: The vast search space of protein sequences makes it computationally expensive to achieve convergence between generated and predicted structures. The IMPRESS framework introduces an adaptive design protocol and middleware that couples AI models with high-performance computing through dynamic resource allocation and asynchronous execution. This approach increases design throughput and improves the consistency of protein design quality.

title:
Mimetic Neural Networks: A unified framework for Protein Design and
  Folding
authors: Moshe Eliasof, Tue Boesen, Eldad Haber, Chen Keasar, Eran Treister
reason: Proposes a unified, reversible framework for both folding and design, representing a significant methodological approach in the field's evolution.
summary: Current protein design methods often struggle to leverage the advancements made in protein folding models. The researchers developed MimNet, a reversible graph mimetic neural network that solves protein structure prediction and sequence design simultaneously in a unified framework. Using the ProteinNet dataset, the method demonstrates that improving structure estimation directly enhances protein design performance, surpassing previous state-of-the-art results.

title: Protein Secondary Structure Prediction Using 3D Graphs and Relation-Aware Message Passing Transformers
authors: Disha Varshney, Samarth Garg, Sarthak Tyagi, Deeksha Varshney, Nayan Deep, Asif Ekbal
reason: Focuses on secondary structure prediction using GNNs and Transformers, a component of the broader structure prediction task, representing recent work.
summary: Current protein secondary structure prediction methods often fail to explicitly incorporate 3D structural data, which is essential for understanding protein function. This study introduces SSRGNet, a model that combines pre-trained protein language models with relation-aware message-passing transformers and graph neural networks to capture both sequential and spatial geometric information. When tested on the NetSurfP-2.0 dataset, the proposed model outperformed existing baselines in F1-scores for both 3-state and 8-state secondary structure classifications.

title: Exploring zero-shot structure-based protein fitness prediction
authors: Arnav Sharma and Anthony Gitter
reason: Focuses on zero-shot fitness prediction using structure-based models, representing a recent application/extension of SOTA structure tools.
summary: This research evaluates how different modeling choices for structure-based machine learning models affect zero-shot protein fitness predictions. The study finds that while structure-based models are powerful, they struggle to accurately predict fitness in disordered protein regions where predicted 3D structures are unreliable. The authors conclude that simple multi-modal ensembles serve as strong baselines for performance on benchmarks like ProteinGym.

title:
HelixFold-Single: MSA-free Protein Structure Prediction by Using Protein
  Language Model as an Alternative
authors:

HelixFold-Single replaces MSAs by integrating a large-scale, self-supervised protein language model with the geometric learning components of AlphaFold2 to predict structures directly from primary sequences. The model achieves competitive accuracy with MSA-based methods on targets with large homologous families while significantly reducing prediction time.

title: Quantifying the Role of OpenFold Components in Protein Structure Prediction
authors: Tyler L. Hayes and Giri P. Krishnan
reason: Analyzes components of OpenFold, a major architecture in the field, providing mechanistic insight into current SOTA prediction methods.
summary: This study investigates how individual components within the OpenFold architecture contribute to the accuracy of protein structure predictions. The researchers systematically evaluated each component's impact to determine its necessity across different protein types. They found that while certain components are critical for most proteins, others vary in importance and show a correlation with protein length.

title: Dynamics-inspired Structure Hallucination for Protein-protein Interaction Modeling
authors: Fang Wu, Stan Z. Li
reason: Pushes the edge of PPI modeling by integrating dynamic variations and structure hallucination for mutants, a current research direction.
summary: Predicting the impact of mutations on protein-protein interactions is difficult because mutant structures are often unknown and traditional models fail to account for dynamic atomic movements. The Refine-PPI framework addresses this by using a structure refinement module to "hallucinate" mutant structures from wild-type data and a probability density cloud network (PDC-Net) to model 3D geometric uncertainty. Testing on the SKEMPI.v2 dataset demonstrates that this approach outperforms all existing tools in predicting changes in binding free energy.

title:
Enhancing the Protein Tertiary Structure Prediction by Multiple Sequence
  Alignment Generation
authors: Le Zhang, Jiayang Chen, Tao Shen, Yu Li, Siqi Sun
reason: Addresses a specific limitation of current SOTA (AlphaFold2) by using generative models to improve MSA depth for structure prediction.
summary: Protein structure prediction accuracy often degrades when a query sequence lacks a deep multiple sequence alignment (MSA) in existing databases. The researchers developed MSA-Augmenter, a generative language model that uses protein-specific attention mechanisms to create novel, synthetic sequences that supplement shallow MSAs. Testing on CASP14 data demonstrated that these generated sequences retain essential co-evolutionary information, thereby improving the structural prediction quality of AlphaFold2.

title: Protein Folding with Neural Ordinary Differential Equations
authors: Arielle Sanford, Shuo Sun and Christian B. Mendl
reason: Proposes a novel continuous-depth architecture (Neural ODEs) to improve efficiency in structure prediction, representing a new research direction.
summary: Current protein structure prediction models like AlphaFold are computationally expensive due to their many discrete, rigid layers. This research replaces the 48-layer Evoformer architecture with a continuous-depth Neural Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) formulation that uses adaptive solvers to balance runtime and accuracy. While the model does not fully match the original's accuracy, it produces structurally plausible predictions and requires significantly fewer resources, training in just 17.5 hours on a single GPU.

title: Benchmarking deep generative models for diverse antibody sequence design
authors: Igor Melnyk, Payel Das, Vijil Chenthamarakshan, Aurelie Lozano

The results show that Fold2Seq outperforms the other models by producing significantly more diverse antibody sequences while successfully maintaining the intended structural fold.

title: SGNet: Folding Symmetrical Protein Complex with Deep Learning
authors: Zhaoqun Li, Jingcheng Yu, Qiwei Ye
reason: Addresses a specific, advanced niche (symmetrical protein complexes) within the broader field of structure prediction, pushing current capabilities.
summary: Predicting the structures of large, symmetrical protein assemblies is difficult for current deep learning models due to excessive sequence lengths and ambiguity in labeling identical subunits. SGNet addresses this by extracting features from a single subunit and using a specialized symmetry module to reconstruct the entire assembly, reducing computational complexity. Experimental results on a benchmark of symmetrical protein complexes demonstrate that this method effectively models all global symmetry types in quaternary structures.

title:
Proteins with alternative folds reveal blind spots in AlphaFold-based
  protein structure prediction
authors: Devlina Chakravarty, Myeongsang Lee, and Lauren L. Porter
reason: Identifies current limitations and 'blind spots' in SOTA models like AlphaFold, pointing toward the next frontier of conformational diversity.
summary: AlphaFold often fails to accurately predict alternative protein folds, frequently producing low-confidence results or defaulting to a single conformation based on training data. The researchers identified three specific blind spots: mispredictions of proteins with conformations distinct from training homologs, an overreliance on training sets, and high-confidence errors caused by degeneracies in pairwise representations. These findings highlight the need for new approaches to reliably capture the structural diversity of proteins.

title: DeltaDiff: Training-Free, Physics-Guided Machine Learning for Predicting Mutant Protein Structures
authors: Yajie Cai, Yanbin Wang, Ming Chen
reason: Presents a recent (2026) method for mutant structure prediction using physics-guided diffusion, representing the current edge of the field.
summary: Predicting how single-site mutations alter protein structures is difficult for existing machine learning models because mutant sequences are too similar to their wild-type counterparts. DeltaDiff addresses this by incorporating mutation-aware physical guidance into a baseline diffusion model without requiring any retraining or fine-tuning. The framework successfully captures significant nonlocal conformational changes in three test systems (Chignolin T8P, Novispirin G-10, and BBL D162N) at a fraction of the cost of conventional modeling methods.

title:
Internal-Coordinate Density Modelling of Protein Structure: Covariance
  Matters
authors: Marloes Arts, Jes Frellsen, Wouter Boomsma
reason: Focuses on modeling structural distributions/fluctuations, a recent frontier beyond static structure prediction (AlphaFold2 era).
summary: Predicting the distribution of protein structural states is difficult because complex correlations between internal degrees of freedom often violate physical constraints. This paper introduces a method to model protein densities in internal coordinates by using 3D spatial constraints to induce the necessary covariance structure. The approach enables the scaling of density models to full protein backbones in both unimodal settings for small fluctuations and multimodal settings for large conformational changes.

title:
EMOCPD: Efficient Attention-based Models for Computational Protein
  Design Using Amino Acid Microenvironment
authors:

summary: Traditional computational protein design methods are often inefficient and struggle to extract meaningful information from sparse protein structures. The researchers developed EMOCPD, a model that uses a multi-head attention mechanism and an inverse residual structure to predict amino acid categories based on their three-dimensional atomic microenvironments. EMOCPD achieved test accuracies of 68.33% and 62.32%, outperforming existing methods by over 10% and demonstrating improved thermal stability and expression in predicted mutants.

title: Assessing the potential of deep learning for protein-ligand docking
authors: Alex Morehead, Nabin Giri, Jian Liu, Pawan Neupane, Jianlin Cheng
reason: Focuses on protein-ligand docking and benchmarking rather than the core task of protein structure prediction/design itself.

They found that while deep learning co-folding methods generally outperform conventional algorithms, even advanced models like AlphaFold 3 struggle with novel binding poses and balancing structural accuracy with chemical specificity.

title: Structure-Informed Protein Language Model
authors:

reason: Pushes the edge by integrating structural information into language models to improve functional prediction, a key part of the current SOTA landscape.
summary: Traditional protein language models lack explicit structural supervision, which limits their ability to predict protein functions accurately. This research introduces a method to distill structural information into these models by integrating remote homology detection during pre-training without requiring explicit 3D structures as input. The approach yields consistent improvements in function annotation accuracy for EC number and GO term prediction tasks.

title:
Protein contact map prediction using bi-directional recurrent neural
  network
authors: Yuhong Wang, Wei Li, Hongmao Sun, Kennie Cruz-Gutierrez
reason: A significant pre-AlphaFold era deep learning approach for contact map prediction, representing the transition to DL-based structure prediction.
summary: Predicting accurate 2D contact maps is a critical step for reconstructing 3D protein structures, but traditional computational methods have historically lacked sufficient accuracy. This study proposes a deep learning model combining a bi-directional recurrent neural network with an artificial neural network to predict these maps. When tested on a non-redundant database of protein structures from the Protein Data Bank, the model achieved a prediction accuracy of 0.80, significantly outperforming previous methods.

title: Computational Protein Science in the Era of Large Language Models (LLMs)
authors:
Wenqi Fan, Yi Zhou, Shijie Wang, Yuyao Yan, Hui Liu, Qian Zhao, Le

This paper reviews the emergence of protein Language Models (pLMs), which categorize protein knowledge into sequence patterns, structural/functional information, and external scientific languages to improve reasoning. The review highlights how these models are advancing protein structure and function prediction, as well as practical applications in antibody design, enzyme design, and drug discovery.

title:
Accurate and generalizable protein-ligand binding affinity prediction
  with geometric deep learning
authors: Krinos Li, Xianglu Xiao, Zijun Zhong, Guang Yang
reason: Focuses on binding affinity prediction (ligand interaction) rather than the core task of protein structure prediction or de novo design.
summary: Existing protein-ligand binding affinity prediction models often fail to generalize when encountering novel, unseen proteins. The researchers developed IPBind, a geometric deep learning method that leverages machine learning interatomic potentials to compare the bound and unbound states of complexes. This approach provides robust, generalizable affinity predictions and offers atom-level insights into the binding process.

title: Twin Peaks: Dual-Head Architecture for Structure-Free Prediction of Protein-Protein Binding Affinity and Mutation Effects
authors: Supantha Dey, Ratul Chowdhury
reason: Focuses on predicting binding affinity and mutation effects from sequences, a specialized task within the broader protein modeling landscape.
summary: Predicting protein-protein binding affinity ($\Delta G$) and mutation effects ($\Delta\Delta G$) typically requires complex structural data, which is unavailable for many proteins. This research introduces "Twin Peaks," a dual-head deep learning architecture that uses transformer encoders and cross-attention to predict both values using only protein sequences. The model achieves a Pearson correlation of 0.638 for $\Delta G$ and 0.485 for $\Delta\Delta G$ without requiring any structural information.

title:
Prediction of amino acid side chain conformation using a deep neural
  network

title: DL4Proteins Jupyter Notebooks Teach how to use Artificial Intelligence for Biomolecular Structure Prediction and Design
authors: Michael Chungyoun, Gabe Au, Britnie Carpentier, Sreevarsha Puvada, Courtney Thomas, Jeffrey J. Gray

The project provides a free, publicly available educational framework to increase AI literacy and participation in biomolecular research.

title: PSBench: a large-scale benchmark for estimating the accuracy of protein complex structural models
authors: Pawan Neupane, Jian Liu and Jianlin Cheng
reason: Provides a large-scale benchmark and evaluation metrics for protein complex modeling, which is a key component of the current SOTA landscape.
summary: Reliably estimating the accuracy of predicted protein complex models is difficult due to a lack of large, diverse, and well-annotated datasets for training machine learning methods. The researchers developed PSBench, a benchmark suite containing over one million structural models from CASP15 and CASP16, annotated with global, local, and interface-level quality scores. Testing a graph transformer-based method (GATE) on this benchmark showed it could achieve top-tier performance in ranking model accuracy during blind testing.

title:
Protein Language Model-Powered 3D Ligand Binding Site Prediction from
  Protein Sequence
authors: Shuo Zhang, Lei Xie
reason: Focuses on ligand binding site prediction from sequence, which is a downstream task of structure prediction rather than the core task itself.
summary: Predicting protein ligand binding sites is often limited by the lack of available 3D protein structures. LaMPSite addresses this by using the ESM-2 protein language model to extract residue-level embeddings and contact maps from protein sequences, which are then integrated with ligand atom-level embeddings from a graph neural network. The model achieves competitive performance compared to existing methods that require 3D coordinates, enabling binding site prediction using only protein sequences and ligand molecular graphs.

title: Protein Multimer Structure Prediction via Prompt Learning
authors: Ziqi Gao, Xiangguo Sun, Zijing Liu, Yu Li, Hong Cheng, Jia Li
reason: Presents a recent (2024) method for multimer structure prediction using prompt learning, representing the current edge of the field.
summary: Predicting the 3D structures of protein multimers is difficult because models trained on simple protein-protein interactions (PPI) often fail to generalize to larger, more complex assemblies. The researchers developed PromptMSP, a framework that uses PPI-inspired prompt learning and a meta-learning strategy to bridge the gap between dimer data and large-scale multimer structures. This method achieves significant improvements in accuracy (measured by RMSD and TM-score) and computational efficiency compared to existing state-of-the-art multimer structure prediction models.

title:
From sequence to protein structure and conformational dynamics with
  AI/ML
authors: Alexander M. Ille, Emily Anas, Michael B. Mathews, Stephen K. Burley
reason: Provides a high-level overview of the field, including AlphaFold2 and RoseTTAFold, and discusses the shift toward conformational dynamics.
summary: Researchers aim to predict protein conformational dynamics by leveraging the hypothesis that amino acid sequences determine not just static structures, but also the movement between multiple states. The proposed method involves developing AI/ML architectures trained on protein sequences combined with conformationally-sensitive data, specifically from NMR spectroscopy. This approach seeks to transition from predicting single protein structures to predicting entire ensembles of distinct protein conformations.

title:
Protein model quality assessment using rotation-equivariant,
  hierarchical neural networks
authors:

reason: Focuses on model quality assessment (MQA), a key component of the prediction pipeline, but is not the primary structure prediction method itself.
summary: Selecting the most accurate protein structure from a pool of computational candidates is a major bottleneck in structural biology. This study introduces a deep learning model that uses rotation-equivariant, hierarchical convolutions on a point-based atomic representation to assess model quality without relying on physics-based energy terms or sequence alignments. The method achieves state-of-the-art performance in scoring protein models for the CASP community experiments.

title: AI-predicted protein deformation encodes energy landscape
authors: John M Mcbride and Tsvi Tlusty

summary: Researchers investigated whether AlphaFold2's structural predictions capture the underlying physics of protein folding by measuring the structural strain induced by single mutations. title: Deep Generative Modeling for Protein Design
authors: Alexey Strokach, Philip M. Kim

summary: Traditional protein design relies on hand-engineered features that struggle to capture complex structural and functional relationships. This review categorizes five successful classes of deep generative models that learn protein representations to rapidly propose millions of novel sequences. These models, when paired with discriminative oracles, allow for the efficient selection of candidates with optimized stability, expression, and desired functional properties.

title: G-VAE, a Geometric Convolutional VAE for ProteinStructure Generation
authors: Hao Huang, Boulbaba Ben Amor, Xichan Lin, Fan Zhu, Yi Fang

The authors developed a Geometric Variational Auto-Encoder (G-VAE) that utilizes Deep Residual Networks and a von Mises-Fisher distribution to map protein structures into a low-dimensional latent hyper-sphere. Experimental results demonstrate that the model successfully generates plausible, novel protein structures that differ from the training data and can accurately complete corrupted protein structures.

title:
Linker-Tuning: Optimizing Continuous Prompts for Heterodimeric Protein
  Prediction
authors: Shuxian Zou, Hui Li, Shentong Mo, Xingyi Cheng, Eric Xing, Le Song

This approach achieved a 56.98% interface prediction accuracy on the i.i.d. test set—a 12.79% absolute improvement over the baseline—while performing 9 times faster than AF-Multimer.
